summary: In April 1880 the author and her husband, Captain Andrew Scott-Stevenson, civil commissioner of Kyrenia in Cyprus, set out with a doctor friend to ride through southern and central Asia Minor, then part of the Ottoman Empire. They landed at Beyrout, went on by Tripoli and Scanderoon to Aleppo, and from there rode for three months by Aintab, Adana, Tarsus, Kaisariyeh, Urgub, Nigdeh, Koniah, and Karaman to the coast, returning to Cyprus by boat.

The book is a day-by-day account of the road: hiring horses and muleteers, khans and guard-houses, brigands reported and met, Armenian and Turkish households, missionaries and consuls, the dervishes of Koniah. It includes the author’s views on Ottoman government and on the peoples of the country, which are those of a British official’s wife of her time. The folding map was drawn for the book by Lieutenant Kitchener.

notes_on_text: Transcribed from the copy at George Washington University (Internet Archive: 39020025955066-ourridethrougha).

Printed pages 322–323 were first read by an OCR program (Tesseract), because the Claude models would not transcribe them; that reading was corrected against the page images by a Claude model and then proofread like the other pages.

The folding map “Map illustrating Captain & Mrs. Scott-Stevenson’s Journey in Asia Minor”, drawn by Lieut. Kitchener, R.E., was photographed in two halves; a narrow strip at the fold is missing from the scan, so a few letters of the map’s title and of place-names near the fold are lost. It is shown here as the two halves.
The contents gives Chapter V as beginning on page 69; it begins on page 68.
